title: Abram lets Lot choose (Genesis 13)
hook: to keep the peace, the elder lets his nephew take first pick of the land

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nachmanides on a famine, a fear and a half-truth. Your line was heroes stumble too. Did you catch yourself shading the truth? Day forty.

Abram comes back from Egypt rich: cattle, silver and gold. His nephew Lot, who came with him, has his own flocks and herds and tents. And now there's a problem anyone who has shared a small apartment will recognize. There isn't room for both of them. The land can't bear them dwelling together, the Torah says, and the herdsmen start to quarrel. Abram's shepherds against Lot's. Arguments over grass and water. It could turn into something worse. And Abram is the elder. God promised this land to his offspring, not to Lot. He could simply tell his nephew where to go. Instead, he does something that would surprise anyone who has ever split a pizza, a bedroom or a family house. Today: who picks first.
screen: `TOO MANY SHEEP, NOT ENOUGH GRASS.` → `THE HERDSMEN FIGHT.` → `THE ELDER COULD DECIDE.`

segments.voice: Abram says to Lot, in the old JPS translation: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we are brethren." In Hebrew, anashim achim: we are men who are brothers. Then he points at the whole land. Is it not all before you? If you go left, I'll go right. If you go right, I'll go left. You choose first. So Lot lifts up his eyes and looks. He sees the plain of the Jordan, well watered everywhere, like the garden of the Lord, and he takes it, and moves his tents toward a city called Sodom. The Torah adds one quiet, ominous line: the men of Sodom were very wicked. Hold on to that; we'll come back there. Now notice the eyes. Lot lifted his eyes and chose what looked best. Right after Lot leaves, God speaks to Abram: lift up your eyes, look north and south and east and west. All the land you see, I give to you and your children. Walk through it. What Abram let go of came back to him as a gift, and bigger. The rabbis added their own note. One midrash says the fight started because Lot's shepherds let their animals graze in other people's fields, while Abram's kept theirs muzzled. And the Mishnah gives a name to what Abram does here, though it isn't speaking about this story: Hillel taught, be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace. Pursuing it. Sometimes that means being the one who says: you choose first.
screen: `FOR WE ARE BRETHREN.` · `LEFT OR RIGHT: YOU CHOOSE.` · `LOT LIFTS HIS EYES TO THE GREEN.` · `ABRAM LIFTS HIS EYES TO A GIFT.` · then, large: `LOVING PEACE AND PURSUING PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think about the small daily contests in your life. Who gets the good chair. Which show to watch. Where to eat. Whose turn it is. Who speaks first in the meeting. Pick one that's coming up today. Picture yourself turning to the other person and saying, you choose. Notice what that feels like in your body: tight, or loose? Stay with it. If you pray, you can ask for a generous heart. The bell holds the time.
Anashim achim, Hebrew for men who are brothers, the reason Abram gave up first choice. The elder, who had every right to pick, gives the first choice away to keep the peace between brothers.
Your line: you choose first. Today, in one small contest, let the other person choose first, and mean it. Day forty.

howItsDone: Jews read this story in the Torah portion Lech Lecha; its words "for we are brethren" and Hillel's teaching about loving and pursuing peace are often quoted when family members or neighbors settle a dispute.

fork.setup: you're Abram. your herdsmen and your nephew's are fighting, and God has promised this land to your offspring. what do you do?
options: tell Lot where he can graze.
fork.reveal: he says, let there be no strife, for we are brethren, and offers Lot the first choice. Lot takes the green plain.

original.note: Hebrew: men who are brothers. Abram's reason for giving up first choice.

trapdoor: what you thought: an uncle and nephew split up the land.
what it means: the elder, promised the land, gives up first choice to keep peace, and gets it back as a gift.
what a scholar hears: "lift up your eyes" twice: Lot lifts his to the green plain; God tells Abram to lift his to the whole land.

sources.quoted: Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee, and between my herdmen and thy herdmen; for we are brethren.

notes: Lot's herdsmen grazing in others' fields while Abram's muzzled their animals: Rashi on 13:7 from Genesis Rabbah 41:5. Confirm.
Hillel's saying (Pirkei Avot 1:12) paraphrased as 'be among the students of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace'; not marked as a quotation. Confirm.
'Green like the garden of God' paraphrases 13:10 ('like the garden of the LORD'). Confirm.
Hook mentions a 'family house' as an everyday picture only.

Editor review (2026-10-01): removed 'every family with a shared inheritance knows' and 'surprises everyone' (sweeping claims); removed 'shoving at the wells' (wells are not in Genesis 13; the text says strife); 'the land can't bear them dwelling together' follows 13:6; 'promised this land to him' now 'to his offspring' (12:7 'unto thy seed'); 'green like the garden of God' now 'like the garden of the Lord' (13:10); Hillel's saying no longer presented as drawn from this scene (Avot 1:12 does not mention it).
